summary: King Saud University authors built a LangChain RAG chatbot that plays a non-technical stakeholder in requirements-elicitation interviews. It retrieves from a ~700-word instructor-written scenario document (FAISS, ada-002, top-4 chunks), uses GPT-3 in Experiment 1 and GPT-4 with sliding memory and persona prompting in Experiment 2, and says 'I don't know' outside the document. In Experiment 1 (50 undergraduates, between-subjects), human faculty role-players were rated more realistic, engaging and clarifying on 4 of 10 items. In Experiment 2 (19 master's students, within-subjects, counterbalanced), perceptions did not differ, but two instructors rated the chatbot sessions as having fewer questioning mistakes and better feature lists on all 13 rubric items.

claims.claim: The RAG-based automated stakeholder produced higher-quality elicitation questions than a human stakeholder
claims.evidence: Fig. 8: mean mistake score 2.52 vs 3.63, all nine items p<=.002. Experiment 2 only (n=19). Questions were prepared in small teams but analysed per student. Raters were two RE instructors (ICC .74) scoring typed chat logs vs transcribed audio, so 'blind' rating is doubtful. Nine correlated items were tested with no multiple-comparison correction, and typed chat (questions visible and editable) is confounded with condition.

claims.claim: The automated stakeholder led to more complete and higher-quality feature identification
claims.evidence: Fig. 9: 3.75 vs 2.62 (p<.001) on four ISO 29148-style items. The bot answers only from the same 700-word document that defines the expected features, while §5.1 notes human stakeholders 'extend' requirements as students ask. Completeness against that fixed reference therefore favours the bot condition by construction.

claims.claim: Students perceived invited human stakeholders as more realistic and engaging
claims.evidence: Experiment 1 (GPT-3, n=50): realism 3.71 vs 4.45 (p=.001), engagement 4.14 vs 4.69 (p<.001), plus RE understanding and concept clarity. Experiment 2 did not replicate this (realism p=.063; no item significant). Several questionnaire items are worded 'The automated customer experience...' yet were also used for the human condition.

claims.claim: RAG grounding mitigates hallucinations and inconsistent responses in simulated stakeholders
claims.evidence: Motivating claim repeated in the conclusion. There is no prompt-only or full-document-in-context arm, and hallucination is never measured. The source document is ~700 words and would fit in the prompt outright.

claims.claim: Automated stakeholders are an effective instructional scaffold for early elicitation training
claims.evidence: Only in-session artifact quality was measured. There is no pre/post test, delayed test, or transfer to a live interview, so learning was not measured.

patterns.note: Pre-spec discovery by interviewing a document-grounded bot instead of a person. Compared against a reasonable alternative (human stakeholder): the bot wins on expert-rated question and feature quality in Experiment 2 (n=19, confounded scoring) but loses on realism and engagement in Experiment 1. 57% still preferred the human, and 64% saw the bot as a conditional substitute.

FAISS + text-embedding-ada-002 top-4 retrieval over 300-token chunks, refusing out-of-scope questions. No isolating comparison against prompt-only or whole-document-in-context (the 700-word doc fits easily), so the RAG contribution is untested.
Framed as a skill-building rehearsal tool for novice analysts. No learning or transfer measure, so the skill effect is not shown.
The domain context is an unstructured plain-language persona document, not a card, glossary or contract.
Sliding conversational memory was added in Experiment 2 together with the GPT-4 upgrade and persona prompting, so it is confounded and not evaluated.

methodology.sample: Experiment 1: 50 third-year SE undergraduates (late 2023, between-subjects, random assignment). Experiment 2: 19 first-semester master's students, many with industry experience (2025, within-subjects, counterbalanced order). One ~700-word scenario (iOS app linking parents with child specialists). Students worked in small teams.
methodology.baselines: Non-technical College of Education faculty acting as stakeholders. No prompt-only LLM, full-document-in-context, or non-RAG chatbot arm.
methodology.models: GPT-3 (Exp. 1) and GPT-4 (Exp. 2) via OpenAI API, temperature 0.1; text-embedding-ada-002; FAISS; k=4.
methodology.variance: Item-level means, SDs and p-values (t / Mann-Whitney / paired t / Wilcoxon). 23 item-level tests with no multiple-comparison correction. No CIs or effect sizes for the main contrasts. Rater ICC(2,1)=.74 [.64,.81].
methodology.ablations: None. Model, memory and persona changed between experiments together with the population.

standards.peer_review: Published in Requirements Engineering 31, 14 (2026) per journal_ref
standards.artifacts: Questionnaire and rubric items in the appendix. No code, prompts, scenario document, transcripts or data released.

biases.detail: All objective (expert-rated) results come from Experiment 2 with 19 students in one scenario.
Feature completeness is scored against the same fixed document the bot is restricted to, while humans extend requirements. In-session artifact quality is reported as educational effectiveness.
Raters were said to be blind, but typed chat logs and transcribed spoken interviews reveal the condition. Raters are RE instructors, possibly from the same course.
13 correlated rubric items and 10 questionnaire items were tested separately at alpha .05 without correction.
Students from the authors' own RE course at one university.
One model per experiment, confounded with population and system changes.
No code, prompts or scenario document released.

coi.affiliations: Department of Software Engineering, King Saud University
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own teaching tool in their own course. No commercial interest.

verdict_reason: The study is peer-reviewed, randomized or counterbalanced, and reports rater ICC. However, the objective advantage rests on 19 students in one 700-word scenario, scored against a reference that favours the bot's own grounding, with doubtful blinding and uncorrected item-level tests. The 'RAG reduces hallucination' rationale was never tested. Usable only as weak evidence that a document-grounded stakeholder bot complements, rather than replaces, human domain experts.
applicability: For developers who lack the domain knowledge, a document-grounded 'domain stakeholder' bot could be a cheap rehearsal step before meeting real SMEs. It would answer only from curated domain sources (content rules, contracts, product briefs) and say 'I don't know' otherwise. This study supports it only as a complement: humans exposed ambiguity and extended requirements, which a bot bound to a fixed document cannot do. It does not show better real elicitation or that RAG matters. If the team builds it, two things matter. First, log every 'I don't know' as a gap in the domain docs, which turns rehearsal into knowledge capture. Second, measure on real tickets whether rehearsal reduces clarification rounds with SMEs, instead of trusting rubric scores against the bot's own source.
